claim: An intrinsic reward-related signal—triggered by successful learning in absence of any external feedback—modulated the entrance of new information into long-term memory via the activation of the dopaminergic midbrain, hippocampus, and ventral striatum (the SN/VTA-Hippocampal loop).
source: We recently provided evidence that an intrinsic reward-related signal—triggered by successful learning in absence of any external feedback—modulated the entrance of new information into long-term memory via the activation of the dopaminergic midbrain, hippocampus, and ventral striatum (the SN/VTA-Hippocampal loop; Ripollés et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Ripollés et al., 2016).

claim: The pharmacological intervention modulated behavioral measures of both learning and pleasantness.
source: Results show that the pharmacological intervention modulated behavioral measures of both learning and pleasantness, inducing memory benefits after 24 hr only for those participants with a high sensitivity to reward.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The pharmacological intervention induced memory benefits after 24 hr only for those participants with a high sensitivity to reward.
source: Results show that the pharmacological intervention modulated behavioral measures of both learning and pleasantness, inducing memory benefits after 24 hr only for those participants with a high sensitivity to reward.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects based on reward sensitivity.

claim: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area complex (SN/VTA), along with the ventral striatum (VS) and the hippocampus (HP), form a functional loop (the SN/VTA-HP loop) in the service of learning and memory.
source: Growing evidence both from animal and human studies support the notion that midbrain dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area complex (SN/VTA), along with the ventral striatum (VS) and the hippocampus (HP), form a functional loop (the SN/VTA-HP loop) in the service of learning and memory (Lisman and Grace, 2005; Goto and Grace, 2005; Lisman et al., 2011; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010; Kamiński et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Signals are sent from the HP to the SN/VTA through the VS, which is thought to integrate affective, motivational, and goal-directed information into the loop.
source: In the downward arm of the circuit, signals are sent from the HP to the SN/VTA through the VS, which is thought to integrate affective, motivational, and goal-directed information into the loop (Lisman and Grace, 2005; Goto and Grace, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine is released from the SN/VTA back into the HP, which in turn enhances memory formation and learning through long-term potentiation (LTP) processes.
source: In the upward arm of the loop, dopamine is released from the SN/VTA back into the HP, which in turn enhances memory formation and learning through long-term potentiation (LTP) processes (Lisman et al., 2011; Lisman and Grace, 2005; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine release promotes the creation of stable memories by allowing LTP to persist over time.
source: Within this loop, dopamine plays a critical role, as its release promotes the creation of stable memories by allowing LTP to persist over time (Bethus et al., 2010; Frey et al., 1990; Hansen and Manahan-Vaughan, 2014; Huang and Kandel, 1995; McNamara et al., 2014; Rossato et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Both explicit and implicit reward, and even intrinsic motivational states (i.e., curiosity), can promote the storage of new information into long-term memory through the activation of the SN/VTA-HP loop.
source: In this vein, fMRI research in humans has consistently shown that both explicit (Adcock et al., 2006; Wittmann et al., 2005; Wolosin et al., 2012; Callan and Schweighofer, 2008) and implicit reward (Ripollés et al., 2016), and even intrinsic motivational states (i.e., curiosity; Gruber et al., 2014), can promote the storage of new information into long-term memory through the activation of the SN/VTA-HP loop (see Figure 8 in, Ripollés et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to fMRI research.

claim: fMRI activity within the SN/VTA is usually associated with the release of dopamine.
source: However, although fMRI activity within the SN/VTA is usually associated with the release of dopamine (Düzel et al., 2009 ; Ferenczi et al., 2016; Knutson and Gibbs, 2007; Salimpoor et al., 2011; Schott et al., 2008), neuroimaging studies can only provide indirect evidence of the actual involvement of the dopaminergic mesolimbic system.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neuroimaging studies can only provide indirect evidence of the actual involvement of the dopaminergic mesolimbic system.
source: However, although fMRI activity within the SN/VTA is usually associated with the release of dopamine (Düzel et al., 2009 ; Ferenczi et al., 2016; Knutson and Gibbs, 2007; Salimpoor et al., 2011; Schott et al., 2008), neuroimaging studies can only provide indirect evidence of the actual involvement of the dopaminergic mesolimbic system.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the limitations of neuroimaging.

claim: Administration of dexamphetamine and methylphenidate (which increase dopamine concentrations in the synapsis by blocking its reuptake) can enhance memory and learning.
source: In this vein, several studies have shown that administration of dexamphetamine and methylphenidate (which increase dopamine concentrations in the synapsis by blocking its reuptake; Breitenstein et al., 2004; Whiting et al., 2007; Whiting et al., 2008; Linssen et al., 2014) and specially, levodopa (the immediate precursor of dopamine) can enhance memory and learning in both healthy (Shellshear et al., 2015; Bunzeck et al., 2014; Chowdhury et al., 2012; Knecht et al., 2004) and clinical populations (Berthier et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Levodopa (the immediate precursor of dopamine) can enhance memory and learning in both healthy and clinical populations.
source: In this vein, several studies have shown that administration of dexamphetamine and methylphenidate (which increase dopamine concentrations in the synapsis by blocking its reuptake; Breitenstein et al., 2004; Whiting et al., 2007; Whiting et al., 2008; Linssen et al., 2014) and specially, levodopa (the immediate precursor of dopamine) can enhance memory and learning in both healthy (Shellshear et al., 2015; Bunzeck et al., 2014; Chowdhury et al., 2012; Knecht et al., 2004) and clinical populations (Berthier et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Levodopa is rapidly taken up by dopaminergic neurons, transformed into dopamine and stored in vesicles from which it will be released into the synaptic cleft each time the neuron fires.
source: Levodopa is rapidly taken up by dopaminergic neurons, transformed into dopamine and stored in vesicles from which it will be released into the synaptic cleft each time the neuron fires.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about levodopa pharmacology.

claim: Levodopa leads to a general increase in dopamine available for release in brain areas innervated by dopaminergic afferents.
source: Thus, levodopa leads to a general increase in dopamine available for release in brain areas innervated by dopaminergic afferents.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about levodopa pharmacology.

claim: Risperidone—a dopamine antagonist—interferes with dopaminergic neurotransmission by binding with a group of receptors known as D2 or D2-like.
source: On the other hand, risperidone—a dopamine antagonist—interferes with dopaminergic neurotransmission by binding with a group of receptors known as D2 or D2-like (Burstein et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the presence of risperidone, the transmission of dopamine-mediated signals to post-synaptic neurons will be reduced due to the blockade of the D2 receptor family.
source: Therefore, in the presence of risperidone, the transmission of dopamine-mediated signals to post-synaptic neurons will be reduced due to the blockade of the D2 receptor family.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about risperidone pharmacology.

claim: Participants ascribed correct meaning to 60 ± 10% of new-words from the M+ condition during the encoding phase.
source: Participants ascribed correct meaning to 60 ± 10% of new-words from the M+ condition during the encoding phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In 61 ± 15% of the M- trials, participants correctly indicated an absence of coherent meaning.
source: In 61 ± 15% of the M- trials, participants correctly indicated an absence of coherent meaning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: After 24 hr, participants still recognized the correct meaning of 65 ± 17% of learned new-words during the encoding phase, significantly above 25% chance level.
source: After 24 hr, participants still recognized the correct meaning of 65 ± 17% of learned new-words during the encoding phase [significantly above 25% chance level, t(25)=12.28, p<0.001, d = 2.33; Bayes Factor-BF10- equal to 1.9e + 9]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Participants correctly indicated that 41 ± 22% of M- new-words identified during the encoding phase had no meaning ascribed, significantly above 25% chance level.
source: and correctly indicated that 41 ± 22% of M- new-words identified during the encoding phase had no meaning ascribed [significantly above 25% chance level, t(25)=3.70, p<0.001, d = 0.70; BF10 = 35.38].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The new group of participants, during the placebo session, learned and remembered words from the M+ condition and correctly identified M- words at the same rate as in the previous experiment.
source: This shows that the new group of participants, during the placebo session, learned and remembered words from the M+ condition and correctly identified M- words (i.e. no meaning ascribed) at the same rate as in our previous experiment.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison with previous data.

claim: Subjective pleasantness and confidence ratings on Day 1 were higher for remembered than for forgotten M+ new words in the 24 hr recognition test.
source: Accordingly, in the present study subjective pleasantness and confidence ratings on Day 1 were higher for remembered than for forgotten M+ new words in the 24 hr recognition test [pleasantness, t(25)=2.75, p=0.011, d = 0.42, BF10 = 4.39; confidence, t(25)=4.56, p<0.001, d = 0.68, BF10 = 232.82]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: No difference in arousal ratings was encountered between remembered and forgotten M+ new words.
source: while no difference in arousal ratings was encountered [t(25)=0.20, p=0.835, d = 0.025, BF10 = 0.21].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Intrinsic reward (i.e. derived from an internal monitoring of learning success) had a modulatory effect on long-term memory.
source: In replicating our previous results (Ripollés et al., 2016), these findings confirm that intrinsic reward (i.e. derived from an internal monitoring of learning success) had a modulatory effect on long-term memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: There was no difference in subjective pleasantness, arousal or confidence ratings for M- new-words which were correctly identified during the encoding phase and still correctly rejected in the 24 hr test and those which were not.
source: Regarding the M- control condition, as expected, there was no difference in subjective pleasantness [t(25)=1.40, p=0.172, d = 0.26, BF10 = 0.49], arousal [t(25)=1.28, p=0.212, d = 0.20, BF10 = 0.43] or confidence ratings [t(25)=1.18, p=0.247, d = 0.18, BF10 = 0.38] for M- new-words which were correctly identified during the encoding phase and still correctly rejected in the 24 hr test and those which were not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The percentage of learned words during the encoding phase was higher under levodopa than under risperidone (as compared to placebo).
source: The percentage of learned words during the encoding phase was higher under levodopa than under risperidone [as compared to placebo; t(25)=2.72, p=0.012, d = 0.56, BF+0=8.26].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The drug effect on the percentage of learned words was still present at 24 hr for the total number of remembered new-words.
source: Importantly, this effect was still present at 24 hr for the total number of remembered new-words [t(25)=2.10, p=0.046, d = 0.45, BF+0=2.62; see Figure 1A].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: No significant changes were found for the arousal ratings between levodopa and risperidone interventions.
source: In addition, while no significant changes were found for the arousal ratings [t(25)=0.31, p=0.757, d = 0.049, BF+0=0.26]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The drug effect approached significance for confidence ratings.
source: the drug effect approached significance for confidence ratings [t(25)=2.05, p=0.051, d = 0.51, BF+0=2.40]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The drug effect was significant for pleasantness ratings, where scores for remembered words at 24 hr where higher under levodopa than under risperidone (as compared to placebo).
source: and was significant for pleasantness ratings [t(25)=2.70, p=0.012, d = 0.64, BF+0=7.93], where scores for remembered words at 24 hr where higher under levodopa than under risperidone (as compared to placebo; see Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: There was not a significant effect of drug on the recognition rate.
source: There was not, however, a significant effect of drug on the recognition rate [i.e. the percentage of remembered words in the recognition test of Day 2 compared to those that were learned on Day 1; t(25)=-0.013, p=0.989, d = 0.003, BF+0=0.20].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The pharmacological intervention was able to modulate measures of reward, memory and online learning selectively during the main M+ condition.
source: This suggests that the pharmacological intervention was able to modulate measures of reward, memory and online learning selectively during the main M+ condition
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: For the control M- condition no significant differences between the risperidone and levodopa interventions as compared to placebo were found for the online learning scores on Day 1.
source: As expected, for the control M- condition no significant differences between the risperidone and levodopa interventions as compared to placebo were found for the online learning scores on Day 1 [t(25)=1.53, p=0.137, d = 0.28, BF+0=1.08]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: For the control M- condition no significant differences between the risperidone and levodopa interventions as compared to placebo were found for the total number of correctly rejected M- words at 24 hr.
source: the total number of correctly rejected M- words at 24 hr [t(25)=0.62, p=0.538, d = 0.15, BF+0=0.35]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: For the control M- condition no significant differences between the risperidone and levodopa interventions as compared to placebo were found for the recognition rate.
source: the recognition rate [percentage of words correctly rejected on Day 2, in respect to those correctly rejected on Day1; t(25)=-0.04, p=0.968, d = 0.011, BF+0=0.20; see Figure 1A]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: For the control M- condition no significant differences between the risperidone and levodopa interventions as compared to placebo were found for the subjective ratings of arousal and confidence.
source: or the subjective ratings of arousal [t(23)=1.72, p=0.097, d = 0.45, BF+0=1.46] and confidence [t(23)=0.36, p=0.720, d = 0.10, BF+0=0.28; see Figure 1B; two participants were excluded from the rating analyses after not correctly rejecting any M- word at 24 hr from those correctly rejected during encoding in the levodopa intervention].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: For the pleasantness ratings in the M- condition, the difference was close to significance.
source: For the pleasantness ratings, however, the difference was close to significance [t(23)=2.02, p=0.055, d = 0.40, BF+0=2.32].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The pleasantness ratings for M- trials remembered at 24 hr were not different from 0 at any session.
source: However, it is important to note that the pleasantness ratings for M- trials remembered at 24 hr were not different from 0 at any session [Risperidone mean rating = −0.23, t(23)=-1.03, p=0.309, d = 0.20, BF10 = 0.34; Placebo mean rating = 0.24, t(23)=1.01, p=0.319, d = 0.20, BF10 = 0.34; Levodopa mean rating = 0.30, t(23)=1.20, p=0.240, d = 0.23, BF10 = 0.40]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Participants did not find the M- learning condition particularly rewarding even if the pharmacological intervention slightly modified their subjective ratings.
source: implying that participants did not find this learning condition particularly rewarding even if the pharmacological intervention slightly modified their subjective ratings.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: No significant correlations were found between the M- learning scores and the PAS.
source: As expected, no significant correlations were found between the M- learning scores and the PAS [Learning Day 1 rs = −0.19, p=0.372; number of correctly rejected words during Day 2, rs = −0.34, p=0.097; recognition rate, rs = −0.19, p=0.372].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: No significant linear correlation or inverted U-shape relationship was found for any learning score (M+ or M-) and the weight dependent drug dosage.
source: In addition, no significant linear correlation or inverted U-shape relationship (Chowdhury et al., 2012) was found for any learning score (M+ or M-) and the weight dependent drug dosage (all ps > 0.13).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: For the drug effect for M+ trials, the number of learned words during encoding showed a significant correlation with the PAS (rs = −0.45, p=0.025).
source: However, for the drug effect for M+ trials, the number of learned words during encoding (rs = −0.45, p=0.025), the total number of remembered words during Day 2 (rs = −0.67, p<0.001) and, strikingly, the recognition rate (rs = −0.49, p=0.017), showed a significant correlation with the PAS (all correlations were FDR-corrected at a p<0.05 threshold, see Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: For the drug effect for M+ trials, the total number of remembered words during Day 2 showed a significant correlation with the PAS (rs = −0.67, p<0.001).
source: However, for the drug effect for M+ trials, the number of learned words during encoding (rs = −0.45, p=0.025), the total number of remembered words during Day 2 (rs = −0.67, p<0.001) and, strikingly, the recognition rate (rs = −0.49, p=0.017), showed a significant correlation with the PAS (all correlations were FDR-corrected at a p<0.05 threshold, see Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: For the drug effect for M+ trials, the recognition rate showed a significant correlation with the PAS (rs = −0.49, p=0.017).
source: However, for the drug effect for M+ trials, the number of learned words during encoding (rs = −0.45, p=0.025), the total number of remembered words during Day 2 (rs = −0.67, p<0.001) and, strikingly, the recognition rate (rs = −0.49, p=0.017), showed a significant correlation with the PAS (all correlations were FDR-corrected at a p<0.05 threshold, see Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The dopaminergic pharmacological intervention induced greater memory and accuracy benefits/deficits in those participants with high sensitivity to reward.
source: Altogether, this pattern of results suggests that the dopaminergic pharmacological intervention induced greater memory and accuracy benefits/deficits in those participants with high sensitivity to reward.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The drug effect for the recognition rate becomes significant if we divide our participants into high and low sensitivity to reward (i.e. hedonic) groups.
source: Note that the drug effect for the recognition rate, which showed no differences in memory performance when pooling all participants together, becomes significant if we divide our participants into high and low sensitivity to reward (i.e. hedonic) groups [U = 35, p=0.033, η2 = 0.19, BF+0=2.81; groups divided according to the median split of their PAS scores; due to the reduced N of the groups we used a Mann-Whitney non-parametric statistical tests, see Materials and methods, Figure 2B, Appendix 1 and Figure 1-Figure supplementary 1B].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in drug effect for the number of words learned during encoding was present when comparing high/low hedonic groups.
source: This difference was also present when comparing high/low groups for the number of words learned during encoding [U = 33, p=0.024, η2 = 0.21, BF+0=4.34]
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The difference in drug effect for the total number of words remembered on Day 2 was present when comparing high/low hedonic groups.
source: and the total number of words remembered on Day 2 [U = 12.5, p<0.001, η2 = 0.49, BF+0=78.74].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The dopaminergic pharmacological intervention did have an effect in terms of both online learning and subjective pleasantness in our learning task.
source: All in all, these results show that the dopaminergic pharmacological intervention did have an effect in terms of both online learning and subjective pleasantness in our learning task, inducing greater memory benefits in those participants more sensitive to reward.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Dopamine can modulate the entrance of new information into long-term memory.
source: By using a double-blind, within-subject randomized pharmacological intervention during a learning task—guided by an intrinsically regulated reward process—known to activate the SN/VTA-HP loop (Ripollés et al., 2016), we showed that dopamine can modulate the entrance of new information into long-term memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The administration of a dopaminergic precursor (levodopa) and a dopaminergic antagonist (risperidone), increased and decreased, respectively, both the learning rate and the level of pleasantness experienced by the participants during encoding.
source: In particular, the administration of a dopaminergic precursor (levodopa) and a dopaminergic antagonist (risperidone), increased and decreased, respectively, both the learning rate and the level of pleasantness experienced by the participants during encoding, as well as the number of words remembered after a consolidation period (24 hr; see Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The administration of a dopaminergic precursor (levodopa) and a dopaminergic antagonist (risperidone), increased and decreased, respectively, the number of words remembered after a consolidation period (24 hr).
source: In particular, the administration of a dopaminergic precursor (levodopa) and a dopaminergic antagonist (risperidone), increased and decreased, respectively, both the learning rate and the level of pleasantness experienced by the participants during encoding, as well as the number of words remembered after a consolidation period (24 hr; see Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The memory effects induced by the dopaminergic pharmacological intervention were stronger in participants with a higher sensitivity to reward (i.e. more hedonic).
source: Strikingly, the memory effects induced by the dopaminergic pharmacological intervention were stronger in participants with a higher sensitivity to reward (i.e. more hedonic; see Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Successful learning was in itself (i.e. in the absence of external feedback) associated with increased reward processing and heightened activity within the SN/VTA and the VS.
source: In a previous study using the same task (Ripollés et al., 2016), we showed that successful learning was in itself (i.e. in the absence of external feedback) associated with increased reward processing and heightened activity within the SN/VTA and the VS.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An intrinsic reward-related signal induced a higher release of dopamine in the HP, which ultimately resulted in enhanced memory formation due to the well-known role of dopamine in mediating LTP processes.
source: We suggested that this intrinsic reward-related signal induced a higher release of dopamine in the HP, which ultimately resulted in enhanced memory formation due to the well-known role of dopamine in mediating LTP processes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from previous findings.

claim: The SN/VTA-HP loop should specially enhance delayed memory.
source: The memory effects reported here (after a 24 hr consolidation period) are also in agreement with the prediction that the SN/VTA-HP loop should specially enhance delayed memory (Lisman and Grace, 2005; Lisman et al., 2011; Adcock et al., 2006; Wittmann et al., 2005; Wolosin et al., 2012; Murayama and Kitagami, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine had an additional role during online learning on Day 1: participants not only learned more words (i.e. they performed better) under levodopa than under risperidone, but also found the learning experience more rewarding when potentiating, rather than hindering, dopaminergic synaptic signaling.
source: In addition to the delayed memory effects reported, here we show that dopamine had an additional role during online learning on Day 1: participants not only learned more words (i.e. they performed better) under levodopa than under risperidone, but also found the learning experience more rewarding when potentiating, rather than hindering, dopaminergic synaptic signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Dopamine improves feedback-based learning in humans.
source: This result is in accord with previous work demonstrating that dopamine improves feedback-based learning in humans (de Vries et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Internally generated signals of self-performance—driven by mesolimbic areas and in absence of external feedback—can guide and improve perceptual learning in humans.
source: and also with research showing that internally generated signals of self-performance—driven by mesolimbic areas and in absence of external feedback—can guide and improve perceptual learning in humans (Daniel and Pollmann, 2012; Daniel and Pollmann, 2014; Guggenmos et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Internally generated signals of self-performance can guide and improve song learning (i.e. motor performance) in songbirds.
source: and song learning (i.e. motor performance) in songbirds (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The level of dopamine directly affected the reward value or the salience of the learning outcome in our task (i.e. learning was more enjoyable), prompting participants to be more motivated and to perform better.
source: An interesting interpretation of our results is therefore that the level of dopamine directly affected the reward value or the salience (Knecht et al., 2004) of the learning outcome in our task (i.e. learning was more enjoyable), prompting participants to be more motivated (Murty and Adcock, 2014) and to perform better.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the results.

claim: The VS, through its connections to the prefrontal cortex (PFC), is located in a perfect anatomical position to add information about the relevance, salience and motivational value of the stimuli to be learned into the SN/VTA-HP loop.
source: The VS, through its connections to the prefrontal cortex (PFC; Lehéricy et al., 2004; Cummings, 1993; Alexander et al., 1986), is located in a perfect anatomical position to add information about the relevance, salience and motivational value (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2008) of the stimuli to be learned into the SN/VTA-HP loop.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research and established knowledge.

claim: Both the VS and the PFC are known to contain and receive dopaminergic receptors and projections.
source: As both the VS and the PFC are known to contain and receive dopaminergic receptors and projections (Haber and Knutson, 2010), dopamine might be able to alter this input, thus modulating the perceived reward underpinning the learning processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Dopamine might be able to alter the input from the VS to the SN/VTA-HP loop, thus modulating the perceived reward underpinning the learning processes.
source: As both the VS and the PFC are known to contain and receive dopaminergic receptors and projections (Haber and Knutson, 2010), dopamine might be able to alter this input, thus modulating the perceived reward underpinning the learning processes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference.

claim: Anhedonia is associated with both reduced activity and connectivity between regions within the mesolimbic reward pathway (especially between the VS and the SN/VTA).
source: This, together with the significant correlation between the PAS and the memory and learning scores (see Figure 2), is also in agreement with previous studies showing that anhedonia is associated with both reduced activity and connectivity between regions within the mesolimbic reward pathway (especially between the VS and the SN/VTA; Keller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The benefit in performance was driven by the suggested role of dopamine in working memory and attention.
source: An alternative explanation, which cannot be fully ruled out, is that the benefit in performance was driven by the suggested role of dopamine in working memory and attention (Surmeier, 2007; Brozoski et al., 1979; Linssen et al., 2014; Drijgers et al., 2012; Mehta and Riedel, 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citations to previous research.

claim: The learning enhancement was partially driven by reward-related and dopamine-dependent processes.
source: However, the fact that no significant learning or memory benefits were induced in the control M- condition and, especially, the relationship between the learning improvements during the encoding phase and the participants' sensitivity to reward (for a similar effect, see Ferreri and Rodriguez-Fornells, 2017), suggest that the learning enhancement was partially driven by reward-related and dopamine-dependent processes (Diehl and Gershon, 1992; Nieoullon and Coquerel, 2003; de Vries et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The cognitive effects caused by the blockade of D2 receptors have usually been studied in the treatment of schizophrenia.
source: The cognitive effects caused by the blockade of D2 receptors have usually been studied in the treatment of schizophrenia (Rabella et al., 2016; Désaméricq et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Antipsychotic drugs (including risperidone) sometimes improve cognitive function.
source: with antipsychotic drugs (including risperidone) sometimes improving cognitive function (Keefe et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Antipsychotic drugs (including risperidone) also lead to impairments in several cognitive domains, including executive functions and memory.
source: but also leading to impairments in several cognitive domains (Sakurai et al., 2013), including executive functions and memory (Uchida et al., 2009; Hori et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Levodopa intake has been related to improvements in feedback-based grammar learning.
